questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman was admitted to the ICU with suspected bacterial meningitis and was placed on empirical therapy with ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Neisseria meningitidis on day 2. The patient had been on antibiotics for 48 hours.
questions.lead_in: What are the most appropriate infection prevention precautions?

options.text: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure side room

questions.explanation: Continue standard precautions Neisseria meningitidis is transmitted person-to-person by respiratory droplets, which travel about 3–6 feet before being removed from the air by the force of gravity. Patients with suspected bacterial meningitis are placed on droplet precautions. After 24 hours of effective therapy, patients with meningitis due to N. meningitidis are no longer considered contagious. In this case, the patient had been treated for greater than 24 hours, and precautions were no longer indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q42

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of fever, headache, and malaise with a few-hour history of severe shortness of breath and chest pain. She was a laboratory worker. On examination, the patient looked unwell. Her heart rate was 120 beats/minute, her blood pressure was 82/46 mmHg, and her respiratory rate was 38 breaths/minute, with oxygen saturations of 92% on 15 liters of oxygen. Investigations: Arterial blood gases showed type 1 respiratory failure CXR: multilobar consolidation with bilateral small pleural effusions Blood cultures: short gram-negative rods seen
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Gentamicin and ciprofloxacin The clinical findings and the occupation of the patient should prompt consideration of a diagnosis such as anthrax or pneumonic plague. Anthrax may cause pleural effusions but is commonly associated with a widened mediastinum and may have clear lung fields; plus the Gram stain does not fit. Both the clinical, radiographic and microscopy results are consistent with infection by Yersinia pestis , the cause of plague. D (gentamicin and ciprofloxacin in combination) is the correct treatment for pneumonic plague. Answer A (benzylpenicillin + meropenem + linezolid) would be the correct treatment for pulmonary anthrax.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q44

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student was found unconscious by his college roommate. He was taken to the emergency room. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures grew Neisseria meningitidis . His roommate received the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine one year ago.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate intervention for the roommate?

options.text: Booster vaccination with the conjugate vaccine
Vaccination with the meningococcal serogroup b vaccine

questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis The meningococcal conjugate vaccine only provides protection against serogroups A, C, Y, W135. Chemoprophylaxis is necessary for contacts of patients with invasive meningococcal disease. If this is identified to be an outbreak due to meningococcal serogroup b, vaccination against serogroup b may be recommended at that point but does not have a role in immediate postexposure prophylaxis. Options for prophylaxis include rifampin, ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and ciprofloxacin.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q43

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman developed meningococcemia. She had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and had an episode of meningococcal meningitis at 12 years of age.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.explanation: CH50 Recurrent Neisseria infections are a red flag for complement deficiencies, and the past medical history of SLE is another clue toward this diagnosis. The best screening test is CH50. This is a screening test for deficits in either the classic or terminal complement pathways. It tests the functional ability of complement components to lyse antibody-coated sheep red blood cells and is sensitive to a decrease, absence, or inactivity of components in the pathway.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q40

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was reviewed prior to treatment with eculizumab, a complement inhibitor. He was known to have paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and had failed treatment with plasma exchanges.
questions.lead_in: What is the most important immunization to arrange before treatment?
questions.explanation: Meningococcal ACWY and menB There is a boxed warning on the eculizumab due to meningococcal infections which may be fatal or life-threatening. Eculizumab recipients are 1000–2000× increased risk of meningococcal infections compared to healthy individuals. Therefore there is a strong recommendation to vaccinate against meningococcus at least 2 weeks prior to the initiation of eculizumab. If they cannot be vaccinated 2 weeks prior, they should receive antibiotic prophylaxis until 2 weeks after vaccination. Patients are also at risk for infections due to other encapsulated organisms, and the patients are likely to have chronic renal failure, so other vaccinations that should be considered are influenza, Hib, and pneumococcal vaccines, but meningococcal vaccine is imperative.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q39

questions.question: What do you do with the following contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis: a triage nurse; a brother who was vaccinated for meningococcus and slept over six days ago; and a pregnant girlfriend?
questions.question_raw: What do you do with the following contacts of patient with meningitis: Triage nurse; Brother who was vaccinated for meningococcus slept over six days ago; Pregnant girlfriend

parts.text: What do you do with the following contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis: a triage nurse; a brother who was vaccinated for meningococcus and slept over six days ago; and a pregnant girlfriend?

parts_raw.text: What do you do with the following contacts of patient with meningitis

questions.model_answer: Chemoprophylaxis is indicated only for close contacts (prolonged contact within ~3 feet, or direct exposure to oral/nasal secretions) exposed in the week before onset, regardless of prior vaccination. (1) Triage nurse: no prophylaxis — routine care/taking vitals is not intimate exposure to secretions (prophylaxis only for HCWs with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, intubation, or airway/secretion contact). (2) Brother who slept over 6 days ago: close household contact — give chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or single-dose ceftriaxone); prior vaccination does not exempt him. (3) Pregnant girlfriend: intimate/household contact — give chemoprophylaxis with ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 (rifampin and ciprofloxacin avoided in pregnancy).

cohort_answer.text:
Chemoprophylaxis should be offered to all persons having close contact with an IMD case during the infectious period (7 days before onset of symptoms - 24 hours after initiation of effective treatment) regardless of their immunization status. Rifampin/cipro for adults and CTX for pregnancy and kids.

Brother who was vaccinated for meningococcus slept over six days ago: Prophylaxis indicated
Pregnant girlfriend: Prophylaxis indicated

parts.text: What are 2 things to do immediately?
It is confirmed as Neisseria meningitidis. What 2 things do you need to follow up with?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 things to do immediately?
It is confirmed as N. meningitidis. What 2 things do you need to follow-up with?

questions.model_answer: a) Two immediate actions: (1) Start empiric antibiotics without delay — ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h (with vancomycin ± ampicillin until pathogen confirmed), as invasive meningococcal disease is a medical emergency. (2) Institute droplet precautions in addition to standard precautions. b) Two follow-up actions once N. meningitidis confirmed: (1) Notify public health and arrange chemoprophylaxis for close contacts exposed in the prior week. (2) Discontinue droplet precautions after 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy; narrow treatment to a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime).

cohort_answer.text: Initiate droplet + standard precautions; Start CTX 2g IV q12h. || Contact Public Health; Close contacts exposure for PEP; Discontinue droplet precautions after 24hrs of appropriate abx.

questions.question: Explain why a vaccine against Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B has been difficult to develop.
questions.question_raw: Men B – why hard to make vaccine

parts.text: Explain why a serogroup B meningococcal vaccine has been difficult to develop.

parts_raw.text: Men B – why hard to make vaccine

questions.model_answer: The serogroup B capsule is alpha(2-8)-linked polysialic acid, structurally identical to polysialylated neural cell adhesion molecule on human fetal and neuronal tissue. It is therefore poorly immunogenic (tolerance to self) and raising antibody carries a theoretical risk of autoimmunity, so capsule-based conjugate vaccines are not feasible. Vaccines instead had to be built from subcapsular protein antigens (outer membrane vesicles, factor H binding protein, NadA, NHBA), which are antigenically variable and strain-specific, so coverage depends on circulating strains and must be estimated by assays such as MATS rather than by serogroup alone.

cohort_answer.text: Antigenic mimicry of the serogroup B polysaccharide capsule, which is composed of polysialic acid structures similar to those expressed on human neuronal cells.

questions.question: Meningococcus serogroup B vaccine.
questions.question_raw: 5. Meningococcus B

parts.text: Why is it so difficult to make an effective vaccine?
What conditions is this vaccine indicated in?

parts_raw.text: a) Why is it so difficult to make an effective vaccine?
b) What conditions is this vaccine indicated in?

questions.model_answer: a) The serogroup B capsule is an (α2→8)-linked polysialic acid that closely resembles human neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM) and other host antigens; it is therefore poorly immunogenic and carries a theoretical risk of autoimmunity, so it cannot be used as a capsular vaccine target (unlike A/C/W/Y). MenB vaccines instead use semiconserved surface proteins identified by reverse vaccinology (FHbp, NadA, NHBA) ± a PorA-containing outer membrane vesicle preparation (e.g., Bexsero/MenB-4C, Trumenba/MenB-FHbp). b) Indicated for persons ≥10 years at increased risk: (1) persistent (terminal) complement component deficiencies, including those on eculizumab; (2) anatomic or functional asplenia; (3) microbiologists routinely exposed to N. meningitidis isolates; (4) persons at risk during a serogroup B outbreak (e.g., college campuses); also considered in HIV. Routine use is permissive in adolescents/young adults aged 16–23 (preferred 16–18).

cohort_answer.text:
Antigenic mimicry of the serogroup B polysaccharide capsule, composed of polysialic acid structures similar to NCAM (human neural cell adhesion molecule) - not a suitable immune target due to risk of autoimmune damage through molecular mimicry. Vaccines for MenA, C, W, Y induce immune response against polysaccharide capsule; MenB capsule is structurally similar to human glycoproteins like NCAM. 4CMenB (2012) combines fHbp, NadA, NHBA with outer membrane vesicles as first recombinant protein-based MenB vaccine
Complement deficiency (eculizumab); Asplenic; Laboratory workers; During MenB outbreak; Close contact with a case of serogroup MenB. Note: >95% of invasive disease caused by serogroups A, B, C, Y, W135

questions.question: A 27-year-old man has meningococcal meningitis. According to NACI guidelines, what is the prophylaxis for each of the following scenarios (note there are immunoprophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis options)?

Q6 (2011 PM)
27M has meningococcal meningitis.
According to NACI guidelines, what is prophylaxis for the following sceniarios: (note there is immunoprophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis options)

parts.text: A nurse who took his blood pressure.
A brother who slept at his house 6 days ago.
His girlfriend who is pregnant — which prophylaxis can you give her?

parts_raw.text: A) RN who took his BP
B) Brother who slept at his house 6d ago
C) His gf who is pregnant, which ppx can you give her?

questions.model_answer: a) Nurse who took his BP: does not meet the close-contact definition (no prolonged <3-foot exposure or contact with oral/nasal secretions) — no chemoprophylaxis or immunoprophylaxis. b) Brother who slept at the house 6 days ago: household close contact — chemoprophylaxis with rifampin or ciprofloxacin (or single-dose ceftriaxone); add immunoprophylaxis if a vaccine-preventable serogroup is identified. c) Pregnant girlfriend: close contact — chemoprophylaxis with ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1 (rifampin and ciprofloxacin avoided in pregnancy); immunoprophylaxis if a vaccine-preventable serogroup is identified.
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter supports the close-contact definition, chemoprophylaxis agents, and ceftriaxone in pregnancy; the specific NACI immunoprophylaxis rule (vaccinate contacts when the serogroup is vaccine-preventable) is a Canadian NACI/PHAC recommendation.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Does not meet definition for close contact. No post-exposure chemo- or immuno-prophylaxis required.

B) Meets definition of close contact. Requires chemoppx with either rifampin or ciprofloxacin. Requires immunoppx if serogroup identified and IMD is vaccine preventable.

C) Meets defn for close contact. Requires chemoppx with Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 dose (other drugs contra-indicated). Requires immunoppx if serogroup identified and IMD is vaccine preventable. Conjugate quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine and meningococcus B vaccine should be considered in pregnancy if indicated (e.g. high risk medical condition, travel to high risk area, post-exposure prophylaxis, outbreak); not studied in pregnancy but no theoretical reason to suspect adverse events.

questions.question: Meningococcal vaccines.
questions.question_raw: Meningococcal vaccines

parts.text: Which meningococcal vaccines are available in Canada?
What considerations would you have in using them in an outbreak situation?

parts_raw.text: Which are available in Canada?
What considerations would you have in using in an outbreak situation?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three classes. (1) Monovalent serogroup C conjugate (Men-C-C): Menjugate, NeisVac-C — routine infant/toddler programs. (2) Quadrivalent A, C, Y, W-135 conjugate (Men-C-ACYW): Menactra, Menveo, Nimenrix, MenQuadfi — adolescent programs and high-risk groups (asplenia, complement deficiency including eculizumab/ravulizumab, HIV, travellers to the meningitis belt or Hajj, laboratory workers). (3) Serogroup B protein-based: 4CMenB (Bexsero, from 2 months of age) and MenB-fHbp (Trumenba, 10–25 years). A pentavalent MenABCWY (Penbraya) is also licensed. Plain polysaccharide quadrivalent vaccine is largely obsolete in Canada.

b) (1) Identify the outbreak serogroup by culture/PCR typing — this dictates which product is used, and for MenB whether the strain's antigens are predicted to be covered (MATS/gMATS or fHbp typing). (2) Define the outbreak population and age range — product licensure differs by age (Trumenba 10–25 years; Bexsero from infancy; Men-C-ACYW products vary). (3) Vaccination history and need for a booster or a second dose — MenB requires a 2-dose primary series, so protection is not immediate; the outbreak may still be ongoing when doses are due. (4) Timing and logistics: vaccine takes 1–2 weeks to protect, so chemoprophylaxis of close contacts and case-finding remain the immediate control measures; vaccination is for longer-term interruption of transmission. (5) Special populations: pregnancy and breastfeeding (conjugate vaccines may be given when indicated), immunocompromised hosts requiring extra doses, and contraindications/allergy. (6) Public health coordination — vaccine supply, defining the target cohort, and communication.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI meningococcal vaccine statement; Canadian products include MenQuadfi and pentavalent MenABCWY in addition to those the cohort lists.

cohort_answer.text: A) Conjugated meningococcal C (Men-C-C): Menjugate Liquid, NeisVac-C. Quadrivalent conjugated (Men-C-ACYW): Menactra, Menveo, Nimenrix. Meningococcal B (4CMenB and MenB-fHBP): Bexsero (4CMenB, can start infancy), Trumenba (fHBP, 10-25yo). B) Serogroup causing the outbreak; age of those being vaccinated; vaccination status; pregnancy/breastfeeding status.

questions.question: Regarding the 2 meningococcal serogroups associated with the Hajj pilgrimage, how are they related to each other?

parts.text: How are they related to each other?

parts_raw.text: B) How are they related to each other?

questions.model_answer: Both serogroups A and W (W-135) are epidemic/outbreak-prone meningococci historically linked to the Hajj, and both are covered by the quadrivalent A/C/Y/W polysaccharide or conjugate vaccine that is required (within 3 years for polysaccharide, 5 years for conjugate) for a Hajj or Umrah visa. Serogroup A is the classic African meningitis-belt epidemic strain; W-135 emerged as a Hajj-associated epidemic strain in 2000–2001.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort's framing (not included in routine vaccines) is off for the Hajj context; A and W are both epidemic-prone and both included in the required quadrivalent ACWY vaccine per the text.

cohort_answer.text: Not included in routine vaccines (last year's answer, noted as possibly not quite correct). A and W available as a single vaccine. A and W rarely cause meningococcal disease in US (Mandell's). Both can cause epidemics (as can C), especially in African meningitis belt

questions.question: Two meningococcal serogroups have historically been associated with the Hajj pilgrimage.
questions.question_raw:
Q47 (2009 AM)
2 meningococcal strains associated with Hajj pilgrimage

parts.text: How has vaccination changed this?

parts_raw.text: C) How has vaccination changed this?

questions.model_answer: a) Historically Hajj outbreaks were caused by serogroups A and C, prompting a mandatory A/C polysaccharide vaccine requirement in 1986. After large serogroup W (W-135) outbreaks in 2000-2001, a quadrivalent A, C, Y, W vaccine (polysaccharide within 3 years or conjugate within 5 years) became a requirement for a Hajj/Umrah visa; arrivals from the African meningitis belt also receive ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis at entry. As a result, vaccine-serogroup (A, C, W) disease and carriage have fallen dramatically (carriage now <5% in pilgrims, 0-0.6% in returning pilgrims), so residual/emerging disease is now driven by non-vaccine serogroups, chiefly B and serogroup X from the meningitis belt.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-vaccine era, meningitis caused more frequently by 5 serogroups (A, B, C, W-135, Y), with B and C the majority. After vaccine C implementation, serogroup C became rare, more B seen, Y second in Canada. For Hajj, quadrivalent (A,C,Y,W) vaccine mandatory led to more non-vaccine serotypes seen: B (worldwide) and X (from Africa meningitis belt)

questions.question: Meningococcal meningitis prophylaxis. What advice do you need to give health care workers?
questions.question_raw:
Q48 (2004 PM)
Meningococcal meningitis ppx

parts.text: Health care workers - what advice do you need to give?

parts_raw.text: A) Health care workers – what advice do you need to give?

questions.model_answer: a) Most hospital personnel are not at increased risk and should NOT receive chemoprophylaxis. Prophylaxis is indicated only for staff with intimate/unprotected exposure to the patient's respiratory secretions - e.g. mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, endotracheal intubation, or airway management/suctioning without a mask before 24 hours of effective therapy. Give it as soon as possible (ideally <24 h; not useful beyond 14 days). Routine care, and the use of standard plus droplet precautions until 24 h of effective antibiotics, does not warrant prophylaxis. Microbiologists handling N. meningitidis isolates should instead be vaccinated.

cohort_answer.text: Only require chemoppx if intensive unprotected contact (without wearing a mask) with infected patient (intubating, resuscitating, closely examining the oropharynx)

questions.question: Meningococcal meningitis prophylaxis. Who is considered a close contact in the community?
questions.question_raw:
Q48 (2004 PM)
Meningococcal meningitis ppx

parts.text: Who is considered a close contact in the community?

parts_raw.text: B) Who is considered a close contact in the community?

questions.model_answer: a) Close contacts (exposed in the week before onset) who warrant chemoprophylaxis are: (1) household members and persons sharing the same living quarters/sleeping arrangements, particularly young children; (2) daycare, nursery school or child-care contacts and frequent playmates of young children; (3) close social contacts directly exposed to the patient's oral/nasal secretions (kissing, sharing eating/drinking utensils or toothbrushes, mouth-to-mouth resuscitation); (4) airline passengers seated directly next to the case on a flight lasting more than 8 hours; (5) health care professionals with intimate exposure (airway management/contact with respiratory secretions). School, transportation, and office contacts are not included unless they meet these criteria.

cohort_answer.text: Household contacts; Persons who share sleeping arrangements; Persons with direct contact of nose/mouth with oral/nasal secretions of case; HCW with intensive unprotected contact; Children and staff in child care settings; Airline passengers sitting directly on either side of the case with flight time >8h

questions.question_raw:
Q48 (2004 PM)
Meningococcal meningitis ppx

parts.text: What should they be given?

parts_raw.text: C) What should they be given?

questions.model_answer: a) Any one of: (1) Rifampin - adults 600 mg PO q12h for 2 days (avoid in pregnancy; reduces oral-contraceptive efficacy; stains contact lenses/secretions; risk of resistance); (2) Ceftriaxone - single IM dose (250 mg adults/>15 yr, 125 mg <15 yr); preferred agent in pregnancy; (3) Ciprofloxacin - single 500 mg PO dose (adults; not routine <18 yr or in pregnancy/lactation); (4) Azithromycin - single 500 mg PO dose. All are ~90-95% effective at eradicating nasopharyngeal carriage and should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.

questions.question: List the conditions and circumstances in which meningococcal serogroup B vaccine is indicated or may be considered.
questions.question_raw: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

parts.text: List the conditions and circumstances in which meningococcal B vaccine is indicated or may be considered, including complement deficiency or eculizumab use, asplenia, laboratory workers, and serogroup B outbreaks.

parts_raw.text: Conditions indicated in – complement deficiency (eculizumab), asplenic, laboratory workers, during menB outbreak, circumstances when could be considered (ie/ outbreak…)

questions.model_answer:
Recommended (high risk of invasive meningococcal disease):
(1) Persistent complement component deficiency (C3, C5-C9, properdin, factor D, factor H) or treatment with a complement inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab).
(2) Anatomic or functional asplenia, including sickle cell disease.
(3) Laboratory or industrial workers routinely exposed to Neisseria meningitidis isolates.
(4) Close contacts of a case of serogroup B invasive meningococcal disease (as adjunct to chemoprophylaxis), and persons in a defined serogroup B outbreak or hyperendemic setting.
May be considered: travellers to areas with serogroup B outbreaks, adolescents and young adults (including post-secondary students in residence) after shared clinical decision making, and recipients of hematopoietic stem cell transplant or those with HIV where local guidance supports it.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI meningococcal statement and ACIP MenB recommendations (shared clinical decision making for adolescents 16-23 years).

questions.model_answer: a) The complement system — eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds C5 and blocks the terminal complement pathway (membrane attack complex, C5–C9), impairing serum bactericidal and opsonophagocytic defense. b) The arthritis-dermatitis (fever, pustular/vesicular rash, arthritis) picture points to a Neisseria: (1) Neisseria gonorrhoeae (disseminated gonococcal infection) and (2) Neisseria meningitidis — both cause the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome and both are strongly favored by terminal complement blockade. c) Ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin) is first-line for both. d) (1) Quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) and (2) serogroup B meningococcal vaccine (MenB).

questions.model_answer: a) Neisseria meningitidis — terminal complement blockade by eculizumab confers a >300/100,000 risk of meningococcal disease. b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (reactivation TB) — B-cell depletion plus latent infection in an immigrant from an endemic region. c) Streptococcus pneumoniae — humoral/antibody deficiency of myeloma predisposes to encapsulated pneumococcal pneumonia. d) Capnocytophaga canimorsus — fulminant sepsis after a dog bite in an asplenic host.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part (a) is addressed by this chapter. Parts (b) TB reactivation on rituximab, (c) pneumococcus in myeloma, and (d) Capnocytophaga in asplenia rest on standard host-defect associations (Mandell chapters on immunocompromise/asplenia, IDSA), not this Neisseria chapter.

questions.question_raw: What antibiotic prophylaxis would you recommend (if any):

parts.text: Repeated isolation of group A Streptococcus from a throat swab.
A man who shared a cigarette with a patient who subsequently develops meningococcal meningitis 5 days later.
A contact of a patient with Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.

parts_raw.text: A. Repeated isolation of GAS from a throat swab
B. Man who shared a cigarette with a patient who subsequently develops meningococcal meningitis 5 days later
C. Contact of a patient with Strep pneumo pneumonia

questions.model_answer: a) Repeated GAS throat isolation = asymptomatic chronic carrier: no prophylaxis routinely; treat/eradicate only in specific settings (household/institutional outbreaks, recurrent pharyngitis in close contacts, outbreaks of rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis). b) Shared a cigarette (exposure to oral secretions) within the week before onset: yes — this is a close contact; give chemoprophylaxis (e.g., ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1, or rifampin/ciprofloxacin). c) Contact of pneumococcal pneumonia: no chemoprophylaxis; person-to-person prophylaxis is not indicated — consider appropriate pneumococcal vaccination based on age/comorbidity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part (b) is grounded in this chapter. GAS carrier management (a) and pneumococcal contact management (c) rest on standard IDSA/GAS and pneumococcal guidance, not this Neisseria chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Chronic GAS carrier (asymptomatic) = no. Ppx offered if part of institutional outbreak, outbreaks of acute rheumatic fever/post strep GN, infections recurring in household/close contacts. Cephalexin 250mg QID x10 days, Amox 500mg BID x10 days, Erythromycin 250mg QID x10 days (if ceph allergic), Penicillin 300mg VK QID x10 days (alt)
Incubation period of Meningococcus is 1-10 days, usually less than 4 days. IPAC uses 7 days before illness onset as relevant duration. Exposure to oral secretions confers risk, no duration needed, therefore yes. Would give ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1
Prophylaxis not routinely recommended. Would consider age and medical condition: appropriate pneumococcal vaccination
